prize_parts.citation: for foundational contributions to the theory of nominal rigidities, staggered price and contract setting, and interest-rate policy rules, and to the microfounded framework that underpins modern monetary policy analysis

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: a single-part B014 prize to Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. I tested it again against the chair's questions and the round-1 exchange. The case rests on the common criteria, not on how many members currently prefer it. Calvo's time-dependent pricing, Taylor's staggered contracts and policy rule, and Woodford's welfare-based synthesis are three conceptually separable contributions, each tied to an identifiable originating body of work. Together they form the framework in which monetary policy rules, inflation targeting and policy trade-offs are analysed. The ideas are roughly 25 to 40 years old and have been extended, estimated and criticised for decades, so maturity is not the issue. What the exchange changed is the citation. I now confine it to nominal-rigidity theory, policy rules and the microfounded policy framework, and it makes no claim about forecasting performance, the Phillips-curve slope or the estimated medium-scale model. That narrower wording answers the chair's question about whether the Committee must first settle theory versus estimation. It would honour the originators of the building blocks and leave the estimation strand (Christiano, Eichenbaum, Galí, Gertler, Smets) to be recognised in the background. This is a judgement about which contribution is the origin, not a claim that the later work is minor.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still attribution. Eight names are credited, and any three-person cut omits Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, whose work on the New Keynesian Phillips curve, estimation and medium-scale models made the framework quantitatively usable. A prize for theoretical originators could be read as overlooking the strand that made the models operational in central banks. The framework's empirical performance after 2008 and in the 2021-23 inflation episode is contested, and some members treat that as a caveat on the contribution, not only on the models. Earlier macro prizes (rational expectations, DSGE methods, time-series macro) are adjacent, and the Committee may weigh the marginal contribution of another monetary-macro prize differently. Finally, three members prefer each of B032 and B010 and two prefer B016, with B014 at three, so a prize for B014 would require agreement well beyond its explicit supporters. I treat that as a fact about the process and not as evidence about merit in either direction.

responses.point: Teorell leaves B014 outside his alternatives. He does not dispute its importance for practice, but says that with eight credited names and several equally strong claimants any three-person cut is contestable, and that he cannot defend a particular trio. He also wants the Committee to say how it reads the post-2021 inflation debate.
responses.response: I take the difficulty seriously, but the stated criteria give a defensible trio. They are originality of the building block, separability from the others, and durability. Calvo's pricing device is used in nearly every New Keynesian model. Taylor's staggered contracts and rule are a different and earlier ingredient. Woodford's welfare-based synthesis is a third step that unified them for policy analysis. Galí, Gertler, Christiano and Eichenbaum build on those layers or estimate them. They are essential to the field but are not the origin of any one of the three components. On the inflation debate, I would answer in the citation. It credits nominal rigidities, policy rules and the policy framework, and makes no claim about forecasting. The debate over the Phillips-curve slope concerns parameterisation, not the existence of the mechanism. I accept that his comparison with Autor, Hanson and Dorn is fair on one point: their credited unit is tighter. I weigh breadth of consequence more heavily than he does.

responses.point: Hassler lists B014 as an alternative and asks the Committee to settle whether it honours the theoretical core or the estimated-model strand before treating B014 as ready. He also separates 'overdue', a statement about timing, from the division of credit.
responses.response: I agree that these are different questions, and I accept the correction on 'overdue'. I would answer the first one by choosing the theoretical core and saying so in the citation. The estimated-model strand is a distinct achievement, concerning identification of monetary transmission and quantitative usability, and the three-name cap cannot combine the two without displacing an originator. My answer to his question is therefore yes. I would accept a citation confined to nominal-rigidity theory and policy rules. I would defend Calvo, Taylor and Woodford against a substitution of Galí or Gertler on the stated criteria, not on counts. The one case where I would reconsider is if a majority judges the estimation strand to be the larger achievement. Then the three names would change and I would want to see the argument. I also note that he co-authors with me and that this is disclosed below.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson prefers B032 with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. She argues that Autor, Hanson and Dorn are identifiable co-originators of one empirical programme, with a transparent design and a record of re-examination. She keeps B014 as an alternative because of its severe attribution problem.
responses.response: Her argument for B032 is the strongest competing case on attribution, and I do not want to understate it. The credited unit is tighter than in B014, and I agree that Dorn belongs with Autor and Hanson for a trade-shock citation. I differ on weighting. My first criterion is how far the contribution is the foundation of a framework that others build on, and in that sense B014 has greater breadth and a longer record of testing. I also ranked B032 sixth in my opening, mainly because the task-framework half of the credit rests partly on people outside this ballot (Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu, Restrepo) and the magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects are still debated. The chair asked what would move me. A clear Committee consensus that attribution cleanliness outweighs breadth, together with specific evidence that the exposure designs withstand alternative inference, would move B032 up for me. I do not have that evidence from the materials supplied and cannot claim it.

responses.point: Andersson moved to B014 from B007. He accepts the Calvo-Taylor-Woodford logic but says the inflation episode leaves the baseline Phillips-curve specification more open than the qualitative content, so the citation should not rest on empirical forecasting. He would give Galí more weight than his own proposal does.
responses.response: I accept the qualification and have written it into the citation above. The qualitative content, price stickiness and policy rules, has survived, and the performance of the baseline Phillips-curve specification is more open. The citation should say nothing about the latter. On Galí, I agree his Phillips-curve and policy-analysis work is close to the centre of the framework, and I treat the omission as a real cost of the cap, as he does. I would still keep Calvo ahead of him, since Galí's contribution is built on Calvo pricing. I am also glad that his argument about Gertler agrees with mine. As we both recall, the 2022 prize went to Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig. That is our recollection and I have not verified it independently here. It does not bear on my reasons for leaving Gertler out, which are strand separation and the three-name limit.

responses.point: Fredriksson prefers B010 with Helpman and Melitz, stressing a two-person credit line and a precisely identifiable core. He notes that my B010 ranking raises a risk that Helpman's appearance in other trade candidacies splits support, and that B014 has eight credited names.
responses.response: I agree that B010 has the cleaner credit line, which is why it is my first alternative. Melitz (2003) and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple form a precisely identifiable core, and his proposal to word the citation around selection and reallocation, not welfare magnitudes, is sound. On the chair's cross-candidate question, this is what would move me to B010. If the Committee concludes that no three-person B014 cut can be defended once the estimation strand is acknowledged, B010 becomes my preferred part, because the Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum gap can be handled in the citation wording. I still put B014 first. The Calvo, Taylor and Woodford components are more foundational for a larger field of policy analysis, and the credit problem, though real, is one of omission and not of confusion about who originated what.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee prefers to honour the theoretical originators (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) or the estimation and empirical-synthesis strand (Christiano, Eichenbaum, Galí, Gertler, Smets). A majority for the latter would change the names, and I would want to see the argument.

How much weight the post-2008 and 2021-23 inflation experience should carry. I treat it as a test of model performance, not of the contribution, but members who read it differently have a reasonable view.

Whether B014's attribution problem (eight names, three slots) is judged more serious than the Dorn versus Katz question in B032 or the uncredited Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum lineage in B010. I cannot resolve that comparison from the supplied materials.

Whether B042 should be treated as a fallback. Its two-person attribution is the cleanest on the list, but the collateral channel is better established as theory than as an identified effect, and the overlap with the 2022 prize is unresolved.

The prior-prize facts used in the exchange (the 2022 recipients, Acemoglu in 2024, Krugman in 2008) are members' recollections, not verified here. I have also not independently verified citation counts or priority claims.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to the proposed laureates (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) is apparent from the supplied profile, and none appears among my documented co-authors. I am a frequent co-author of John Hassler (chair) and of Timo Boppart (co-opted member), and an IIES colleague of both. I co-authored with Boppart on the 2018 Myrdal Prize article and the JPE 2020 paper. Boppart and I both prefer B014, and Hassler lists it as an alternative. My long-term co-authors (Smith, Ríos-Rull, Violante, Greenwood, Hercowitz, Tsyvinski, Olovsson, among others) are not credited on any shortlisted ballot. My heterogeneous-agent and macro-inequality work is adjacent to non-shortlisted candidates and I do not rely on it here. I am the secretary in this simulation. These are disclosures, not adjudicated conflicts.
